title: A CAR T gut side effect, a fertility coverage gap, and noninvasive brain stimulation
dek: CAR T cells themselves can inflame the gut after myeloma therapy. California's fertility mandate reached 18 percent of young cancer patients. A 69-person trial tests brain stimulation for low mood. Also: a pancreatic cancer weak spot.

tldr.text: In 158 myeloma patients given cilta-cel, nine developed gut inflammation driven by CAR T cells that had grown into the bowel wall.
Of 903 young patients with cancer in California, 18 percent were covered by the state fertility preservation mandate.
In 69 people with mild low mood, three sessions of brain stimulation at 10 hertz eased symptoms, and 5 hertz did nothing.
In pancreatic cancer mice, blocking the serine enzyme PHGDH made tumours depend on glutamine, and a glutamine blocker then shrank them.
A part of Wernicke's area, long tied to hearing, switches on about a quarter of a second before a word is spoken.

top.title: CAR T cells themselves cause the gut inflammation seen after cilta-cel in myeloma
top.gist: Among 158 myeloma patients treated with cilta-cel, nine developed severe gut inflammation. Biopsies showed it was driven by clones of the CAR T cells, found at 100 times higher levels in blood.

evidence.limitation: One cancer centre, nine cases, and no test of how to treat it. Read from the abstract only.

top.why: Late diarrhoea after CAR T therapy had been hard to explain. Knowing the cause points to biopsy and CAR T cell tracking as ways to tell it from other gut disease.
details: The incidence was 5.1 percent at six months and 5.7 percent overall. Patients with the condition had 100 times more CAR T cells persisting in blood than patients without it.
All nine cases showed one or a few dominant T cell clones. RNA sequencing showed stronger cell-killing and inflammatory programmes in the infiltrating cells than in controls.
The CAR gene had landed in active genes without signs that it caused harmful changes. Few cancer driver mutations were found, which separates this from T cell lymphoma after CAR T therapy.
top.didNotShow: It did not show how to treat the condition, how long it lasts, or whether other CAR T products behave the same way.

terms.def: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel, a CAR T cell product approved for relapsed multiple myeloma.
Immune cells taken from a patient and engineered to carry a receptor that targets cancer cells.
A cancer of plasma cells, the antibody-making cells of the bone marrow.
A group of cells that all descend from one original cell and share its genetic identity.

top.forYou: Engineered cell therapy safety and tissue infiltration, relevant to adoptive cell therapy design.

top.title: California's fertility preservation mandate covered only 18 percent of young patients with cancer
top.gist: In 903 young patients newly diagnosed with cancer at one US centre, 18 percent had insurance covered by the state mandate. Non-English speakers were 64 percent less likely to be eligible.

evidence.limitation: One comprehensive cancer centre in one state, so reach elsewhere may differ. Read from the abstract only.

top.why: Fertility preservation before cancer treatment works, but the law helps few of those at risk. The gap falls hardest on people on Medicaid and people who do not speak English.
details: Ineligibility came from Medicaid (49 percent), commercial plans outside the mandate (37 percent), military plans (9 percent), federal employee plans (2 percent) and no insurance (3 percent).
Among patients whose plans were covered, insurers wrongly said there was no fertility benefit 28 percent of the time. Checking benefits took a median of 45 minutes per patient.
top.didNotShow: It did not measure how many patients actually received fertility preservation, or how the outcome affected later births.

terms.def: Freezing eggs, sperm or embryos before treatment that could damage the ability to have children.
A US public insurance programme for people with low incomes.
A state law that requires insurers to cover a named service.

diagram.caption: Of 903 young patients with cancer, 18 percent were eligible for fertility preservation benefits under the mandate.

sources.label: Journal of Clinical Oncology, Chacon et al.

top.forYou: Health policy and access gaps in oncofertility care.

top.title: Expanding young adult-born neurons strengthens social memory in mice
top.gist: In mice, expanding immature adult-born neurons in the hippocampus recruited inhibitory cells, reduced memory interference and improved social memory. The same expansion of older neurons did not.

evidence.limitation: A mouse study of one memory type. Group sizes were not read from the abstract.

top.why: Adult neurogenesis falls with age. This links young new neurons to inhibition and brain rhythms that consolidate memory, a testable route for age-related memory loss.
details: Expanding 4-week-old new neurons raised activity of fast-spiking inhibitory cells in the CA3 and CA2 regions. Expanding 8-week-old neurons did not.
Recordings showed longer, stronger sharp-wave ripples, brain rhythms linked to memory consolidation. Switching the inhibitory cells on or off showed they were needed for the effect.
top.didNotShow: It did not show any effect in people, or on memory types other than social memory.

terms.def: New nerve cells made in the adult brain, mostly in the dentate gyrus of the hippocampus.
Short bursts of brain activity in the hippocampus linked to storing memories.
Nerve cells that dampen the activity of other nerve cells.
Describes a method that switches chosen cells on or off with an engineered receptor and a drug.

top.forYou: Circuit-level inhibition and oscillations relevant to memory consolidation.

top.title: A scoring system ranks 87 antibody drug targets across more than 32,000 tumour samples
top.gist: Using data from over 32,000 tumour samples, researchers profiled 87 antibody drug targets and built a ReSort score to rank them. It has not been tested in a trial.

evidence.limitation: Computational and model-based matching. Prospective clinical benefit was not shown. Read from the abstract only.

top.why: Antibody drugs are becoming plentiful, and the hard part is choosing the right patient. A shared scoring framework could help match targets and trials.
details: The work covers how often each target is present, how uneven it is inside a tumour, the immune setting, and how well the drug gets inside cells.
The authors report that ReSort agrees with clinical assays and predicts response in patient-derived models, and they built an AI tool for trial matching.
top.didNotShow: It did not show that choosing patients with ReSort improves survival in a trial.

terms.def: A protein on cancer cells that an antibody-based medicine is built to find.
The authors' two-step score for ranking targets.
A trial design that tests several treatments, each matched to a tumour feature.

top.forYou: Target selection and tumour heterogeneity relevant to targeted delivery design.

top.title: A perspective links poor sleep, brain fluid flow and treatment-resistant depression
top.gist: A Molecular Psychiatry perspective argues that disturbed brain fluid clearance, tied to sleep, may keep depression going in some patients, and sets out how to test it in people.

evidence.limitation: A perspective that proposes a hypothesis. It reports no new patient data. Read from the abstract only.

top.why: It turns a vague link between sleep and depression into measurable steps: imaging, sleep tracking and treatment response over time.
details: The abstract notes that the main MRI index, DTI-ALPS, is indirect. In one treatment-resistant depression study, a higher value was partly driven by lower diffusion in the denominator, so each component should be read separately.
It names ketamine, magnetic stimulation and light or sleep-timing treatments as ways to probe the idea, and calls for long follow-up studies.
top.didNotShow: It did not show that fluid clearance causes depression or that changing it helps.

terms.def: A proposed network that moves fluid through the brain to clear waste, most active in sleep.
An MRI measure of water movement along brain blood vessels, used as an indirect sign of fluid clearance.
Depression that does not improve after trying several treatments.

top.forYou: Fluid transport and clearance in the brain, relevant to drug delivery across the brain.

top.title: FDA rejects Capricor's cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy
top.gist: The news site STAT reports that the FDA rejected Capricor Therapeutics' cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Only a feed summary was read, so reasons are unknown.

evidence.limitation: The STAT+ story is behind a subscription. Only a one sentence summary was read.

top.why: Regulatory decisions in rare disease shape what trials must show for small patient groups.
top.didNotShow: It did not show the FDA's stated reasons or the trial data behind the decision.

terms.def: A US health and science news outlet whose main stories need a subscription.
A rare inherited disease in which muscles weaken over time, mostly affecting boys.

top.forYou: Regulatory expectations for cell therapy in small populations.

bench.title: PHGDH Inhibition Confers a Targetable Glutamine Dependency in Pancreatic Cancer
bench.headline: Blocking the serine enzyme PHGDH caused pancreatic tumours in mice to rely on glutamine, which made them sensitive to a glutamine blocker.

evidence.model: Genetically engineered mouse models of pancreatic cancer
evidence.limitation: Mouse models only. Group sizes and survival effects were not read from the abstract.

bench.question: Does the serine making enzyme PHGDH matter at every stage of pancreatic cancer, and can blocking it be combined with another drug?
bench.approach: The team measured PHGDH from early lesions to invasive cancer, lowered it in mice, treated mice with the PHGDH inhibitor BI-9593, then traced nutrients and tested the glutamine antagonist DRP-104.
bench.model: Human and mouse tissue, and genetically engineered mouse models with switchable PHGDH knockdown.
bench.result: PHGDH rose step by step from early lesions to invasive cancer. Lowering it delayed tumour development. BI-9593 cut serine production, killed cells and shrank tumours. Dietary serine and glycine changes did nothing. PHGDH loss lowered ASCT2 and glutamine uptake, and DRP-104 then worked selectively.
bench.limitations: Mouse work read from the abstract only. Numbers, durability and safety of the combination were not checked.
bench.meaning: It suggests pairing a serine pathway block with a glutamine blocker, and shows why single metabolic drugs may fall short.

diagram.caption: In mice, losing PHGDH reduced ASCT2 and glutamine use, which left tumours open to the glutamine blocker DRP-104.

terms.def: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, the most common type of pancreatic cancer.
The enzyme that makes the amino acid serine from sugar.
A protein on cell surfaces that carries glutamine into cells.
A drug that blocks glutamine use in cells.
A method that follows labelled nutrients to see which products cells make from them.

bench.forYou: Metabolic rewiring in the pancreatic tumour microenvironment, relevant to combination design.

bench.title: Temporal interference stimulation targeting the ventromedial prefrontal cortex enhances reward learning and improves depression scores
bench.headline: Gentle electrical stimulation at 10 hertz over a reward area of the brain improved reward learning, and eased mild low mood in 69 people over three days.

evidence.limitation: Mild symptoms, three sessions and 7 days of follow-up. Read from the abstract only.

bench.question: Can stimulating the brain's reward circuit without surgery improve reward learning and low mood?
bench.approach: Brain imaging and modelling in healthy adults found a loop between the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and the ventral striatum. The team then applied 10 hertz and 5 hertz stimulation over the prefrontal area.
bench.model: Healthy adults, then a randomised trial in 69 people with subclinical depression.
bench.result: Reward errors were tracked by alpha and theta waves in the prefrontal cortex. 10 hertz stimulation improved reward learning and reshaped connectivity, and 5 hertz did not. Three daily sessions eased symptoms, with benefits that appeared 7 days later.
bench.limitations: The trial involved mild symptoms, not clinical depression, and only short follow-up. Effect sizes and sham design were not read.
bench.meaning: It supports testing this noninvasive stimulation in larger clinical groups, and shows which frequency to use.

diagram.caption: The study tracked reward prediction errors in a prefrontal and striatal loop and boosted them with stimulation.

terms.def: A way of stimulating deep brain areas through the skull using two overlapping electric currents.
A front brain region involved in valuing rewards and making choices.
A deep brain region that responds to rewards.
Mild low mood that falls short of the threshold for a depression diagnosis.

sources.label: Science Translational Medicine, Wang et al.

bench.forYou: Noninvasive modulation of deep targets, relevant to field delivery in tissue.

method.title: Isolating and profiling lipid droplets from cultured neurons
method.gist: A Nature Protocols paper shows how to enlarge neuronal lipid droplets so they float out of a sucrose gradient, then profile their fats by mass spectrometry in 3 to 4 weeks.
method.useWhen: You want to learn what fats neuronal lipid droplets hold in a neurodegeneration model and need to purify them from primary neurons.

steps.title: Culture neurons
steps.text: Grow primary neurons in culture, as the protocol describes.

steps.title: Enlarge the droplets
steps.text: Block the neuron-specific triglyceride lipase so the droplets grow big enough to separate.

steps.title: Float the droplets
steps.text: Spin the lysate on a sucrose gradient in an ultracentrifuge so the droplets float.

steps.title: Profile the fats
steps.text: Run liquid chromatography and mass spectrometry for lipidomics on the purified droplets.

pitfalls: Neuronal droplets are tiny and rare, which is why they are enlarged first.
Gradient steps, speeds and settings are not listed here. Take them from the protocol.
method.safety: Follow your institution's rules for cell culture, biological material and ultracentrifuges.

terms.def: A small fat store inside a cell, wrapped in a thin membrane.
The large-scale measurement of the fats in a sample.
A machine that spins samples at very high speed to separate parts by density.

method.forYou: Organelle isolation and lipid profiling that transfers to nanoparticle uptake work.

learn.question: What is a reward prediction error, and why does it matter for learning?
learn.answer: It is the gap between the reward you expected and the one you got. Brains use that gap to update their guesses, so surprises teach more than predictable events.
learn.analogy: Like a satnav: it only updates the route when the road differs from what it predicted.
body: A reward prediction error is positive when an outcome is better than expected and negative when it is worse. When the outcome matches, the error is zero and little is learned.
Learning models use the error to adjust what a person expects next time. How fast they adjust is the learning rate, which differs between people.
In today's brain stimulation bench paper, the abstract says activity in a prefrontal and striatal loop tracked these errors and scaled with each person's learning rate.

diagram.caption: A reward prediction error is the gap between expected and real reward, and it drives the update to the next expectation.

terms.def: How strongly a person updates their expectations after each surprise.
The difference between what was expected and what happened.

sources.label: Science Translational Medicine, Wang et al.

curiosity.title: A listening area of the brain also starts every spoken word
curiosity.gist: A small spot in Wernicke's area, long tied to understanding speech, switches on about a quarter of a second before a word is spoken, new recordings in 28 people show.
body: Science News reports that the team recorded brain activity before epilepsy or tumour surgery. The spot, the left posterior superior temporal gyrus, fired as people heard words and just before they tried to speak. Electrical stimulation there just before speech disrupted talking.

It responded more before long words than short ones. In two volunteers with paralysis, experimental implants picked up both what they heard and what they tried to say, which suggests a new target for speech devices.

evidence.limitation: Read from a Science News report of a Science paper, not the paper itself. The recordings came from people having brain surgery.

terms.def: A region on the left side of the brain, first described in 1874, tied to understanding speech.
A device placed on or in the brain that records or stimulates activity.
